text: In which year did the Original Dixieland Jass Band make what is usually called the first jazz record?
explanation: The Original Dixieland Jass Band recorded for Victor in New York in 1917, which is normally cited as the first jazz record.
tip: First jazz record = 1917, Original Dixieland Jass Band.

text: How were jazz records made during the acoustic era (before 1925)?
correct: Performers played into a large horn that made a stylus cut the disc directly
wrong: Performers were recorded by ribbon microphones onto magnetic tape
Each instrument was recorded on its own multitrack channel
Sound was sampled digitally and stored as data
explanation: Acoustic recording had no microphone or amplification. Sound waves travelled down a horn, moved a diaphragm and stylus and cut the groove straight into a disc.
tip: Acoustic era = horn + stylus, no microphone, no editing.

text: Why were bass drums usually avoided in acoustic-era jazz recordings?
correct: Strong low-frequency vibrations could make the cutting stylus jump out of the groove
wrong: They were too quiet to be picked up by the horn
They were banned by record labels for religious reasons
They could not be tuned to the key of the song
explanation: Heavy low-frequency energy caused the stylus to jump. Bass drums were avoided or softened, and a tuba often replaced the double bass.
tip: Acoustic era: no bass drum (stylus jumps), tuba instead of double bass.

text: What is the polar pattern of a classic RCA ribbon microphone, and why was it useful in jazz?
correct: Figure-8 (bidirectional), so two players could face each other at either side of one microphone
wrong: Omnidirectional, so it picked up the whole room equally
Cardioid, so it only picked up sound from one direction
Hypercardioid, so it rejected all sound from the side and rear
explanation: A ribbon microphone has a figure-8 pattern, picking up sound from the front and back and rejecting the sides. This allowed two horn players to share one mic.
tip: Ribbon mic = figure-8 pattern, warm and smooth.

text: How did the length of a 78 rpm disc influence swing-era recordings?
correct: Each side held only about 3 to 4 minutes, so tunes were arranged and edited to fit
wrong: A side could hold over 20 minutes, allowing long solos
Records were always recorded in stereo
Each record had to be recorded in a single take with no rehearsal
explanation: 78 rpm shellac discs held roughly 3 to 4 minutes per side. Swing arrangers tailored their pieces to that length.
tip: 78 rpm = 3-4 minutes a side; long solos were not possible.

text: What did the 33⅓ rpm microgroove LP, introduced in 1948, allow jazz to do?
correct: Release extended performances, up to about 22 minutes per side
wrong: Record in stereo for the first time ever
Record digitally with no surface noise
Replace the need for any microphones
explanation: The LP held far more music than a 78, making extended improvised solos and album-length works practical, as on Kind of Blue.
tip: LP (1948) = up to ~22 minutes a side; albums and long solos.

text: What was a key advantage of magnetic tape for jazz producers?
correct: The best takes could be edited and spliced together, and tape later allowed stereo and multitrack
wrong: It removed the need for performers to play live
It made every recording louder by default
It could only record one instrument at a time
explanation: Tape could be cut and joined, letting producers choose the best takes. It also led to stereo and multitrack recording.
tip: Tape = editing, splicing, then multitrack and stereo.

text: Which describes the recording approach associated with engineer Rudy Van Gelder at Blue Note?
correct: Close-miked instruments, often with tube condenser microphones, giving a punchy, clear, intimate sound with natural bleed
wrong: Distant ambient miking in a huge concert hall
Heavy multitrack overdubbing with artificial reverb
Using only a single omnidirectional microphone for the whole band
explanation: Van Gelder placed microphones close to the instruments and recorded the band live to tape. The result is clear, present and dry, with natural bleed holding the band together.
tip: Van Gelder = close-miked, tube condensers (Neumann U47), live band, punchy and clear.

text: Which best describes the style of Miles Davis' So What from Kind of Blue (1959)?
correct: Modal: improvisation based on scales (modes) rather than fast-changing chords
wrong: Free jazz with no fixed structure or key
Dance-band swing arranged for a big band
Electric fusion with synthesizers
explanation: So What is built on a few modes (D Dorian, then E-flat Dorian) in a 32-bar AABA form, giving improvisers space rather than constant chord changes.
tip: Modal jazz = scales/modes instead of fast chord changes (Kind of Blue).

text: What is unusual about Dave Brubeck Quartet's Take Five (1959)?
correct: It is in 5/4 time, composed by saxophonist Paul Desmond
wrong: It is in 4/4 but played at 300 bpm
It uses no improvisation at all
It was the first jazz record to use synthesizers
explanation: Take Five is famous for its 5/4 time signature and repeated two-chord vamp, with solos including a well-known drum solo.
tip: Take Five = 5/4 time, written by Paul Desmond.

text: How did 1940s bebop differ from swing?
correct: Small combos played faster, harmonically complex, virtuosic improvisation, mainly for listening rather than dancing
wrong: Large dance bands played simple riffs for dancing
It used only electronic instruments
It avoided improvisation in favour of written scores
explanation: Bebop musicians such as Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie played fast tempos with extended and altered chords, in small groups.
tip: Bebop = small combo, fast, complex harmony, virtuosic improvisation.

text: Which technology features are associated with Miles Davis' Bitches Brew (1970) and later jazz fusion?
correct: Electric piano and other electric instruments, plus tape editing, loops and echo by producer Teo Macero
wrong: Only acoustic instruments recorded live with one microphone
Wax cylinder recording and acoustic horns
Fully digital sampling workstations
explanation: Fusion mixed jazz with rock and used the studio as an instrument. Teo Macero edited and assembled long sessions with tape splicing, loops and echo, while players used electric piano and later synthesizers.
tip: Fusion = electric instruments (Rhodes, synths) + tape editing, loops, echo (Teo Macero).
